https://www.egyptindependent.com/us-inte.text: Recent US intelligence assessments indicate Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve by launching a limited attack on an allied country within the next few years, according to three sources familiar with those reports. The intelligence assessments outline several possible scenarios for Russian escalation, ranging from a cyberattack to a small-scale incursion intended to challenge NATO’s unity and commitment to Article 5, which states that an attack on one member is an attack on all, without necessarily crossing the threshold for an allied response, the sources said. While how and when Putin might do so remains an open question, one of the sources said he is most likely to escalate in some way by targeting the Baltics or Poland. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the recent assessments. US and NATO officials believe Putin may choose to escalate against NATO if he is unable to secure a face-saving off-ramp to the war with Ukraine, the sources added, noting the Russian president’s window for choosing his next course of action spans between now and the next few years. Martin O’Donnell, a senior NATO military spokesperson, declined to comment on classified intelligence assessments but said NATO is “always thinking through and preparing for any number of scenarios.” “NATO is watching and we are ready to deter and defend as necessary, which we continue to demonstrate,” he added. There have been numerous instances over the last few years of Russia encroaching on NATO territory. In May, a drone carrying explosives hit an apartment building in Romania as Russian forces attacked a nearby Ukrainian port, injuring two people. And last September, NATO fighter jets shot down multiple Russian drones that had violated Polish airspace during an attack on Ukraine. And just this week, the US assessed that an explosive-laden drone discovered at an airport in Germany overnight on Wednesday belonged to a Russian intelligence service, a US defense official in Europe told CNN. The official said the drone was carrying military-grade explosives; CNN previously reported it was discovered by an airport staff member in a secure area of cargo flight operations. LEIPZIG, GERMANY - AUGUST 5: Police investigators work on the tarmac with a robot capable of defusing explosives near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 5, 2026 near Leipzig, Germany. Airport workers reportedly discovered a drone yesterday on the tarmac near an Antonov at the airport that was equipped with an explosives detonator and an unidentified substance. Additionally, a DHL cargo plane that took off from the airport late last night collided with a small object, causing minor damage. (Photo by Jens Schlueter/Getty Images) Jens Schlueter/Getty Images CNN asked the Kremlin for comment on the US intel assessment on Putin as well as the assessment on the drone. “Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters on Wednesday. “That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario.” Dobrindt indicated Thursday that the drone could be tied to “foreign powers” though he stopped short of providing specifics. The German National Security Council, led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, met on Friday to discuss the airport incident. The intelligence assessments on Russia’s plans also come amid heightened concerns over the US’ munitions stockpile which has been significantly depleted in the war against Iran, and an increase in civilian casualties from Russian long-range weapons. CNN previously reported that nearly 80% of its THAAD missile interceptors — a key missile defense system — have been exhausted in the war compared to pre-war levels, as well as roughly half of its Patriot interceptors. Meanwhile, the UN has said that civilian casualties from Russian long-range weapons increased 60% between January to June, compared to the same period last year. In one night of attacks this week, Russian ballistic and anti-ship missiles killed at least 17 people and wounded dozens more. None of the missiles were intercepted by Ukrainian defenses, CNN reported. Concerns over key munitions and interceptors are impacting the way senior military commanders are planning for potential future conflict, including escalation against NATO by Putin or war with China in the Pacific. President Donald Trump has privately complained in recent days about reports of the US’ dwindling stockpiles due to the war with Iran, including last week at a Cabinet meeting at Camp David, six sources familiar with the meeting previously told CNN. “The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump said on Truth Social late Thursday night. “Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history.” The recent intelligence assessments also come as US-led diplomatic efforts to bring the war between Russia and Ukraine to an end have stalled. Ongoing US and European sanctions against Moscow have had an impact on Russia’s economy but have not stopped Putin’s continued assault on Ukraine.

https://conservativehq.com/post/putin-is.text: http://conservativehq.com/post/putin-is-desperate-cornered-and-hitting-western-leaders-next Putin is desperate, cornered — and hitting Western leaders next by: Bob McEwen, former Member U.S. House of Representatives Oct 05, 2026 Source: Conservative HQ 10/06/2026 putin_tagets_ukraine_train_diplomats Russian President Vladimir Putin is losing. Not just the war he launched on Ukraine in 2022, but any credibility or respect from other world leaders. His invasion of Russia’s former Soviet state should have been over quickly. He failed to grasp that after experiencing independence, Ukraine had no desire to again be controlled by a murderous thug dictatorship in Moscow. Ukraine’s tenacity and ability to innovate have stunned the world and made Putin more desperate, erratic, and aggressive. Putin’s war strategy to this point has been to target innocent civilians, churches, and children and hit at the heart of Ukrainian identity and national pride. In recent weeks, he has bombed shopping centers and grocery stores in order to deplete Ukraine’s food supply heading into the harsh winter months. Now, in his desperation, Putin has scaled up attacks on Western leaders who, thanks to President Donald Trump’s cajoling, have stepped up to the plate, built up their military capabilities, and doubled down in their support for Ukraine. On Sept. 13, Putin ordered the horrific bombing of a Kyiv-to-Poland-bound train that was carrying former U.S. CIA Director and Army General David Petraeus, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, and former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, among other diplomats and journalists. Mitzi Perdue, an 85-year-old reporter, recounts the terrifying night spent scrambling to get away from the burning train amid the overwhelming acrid smoke, maneuvering in the darkness and confusion to hide in the bushes as a drone buzzed above the wreckage. Perdue has traveled to the war-torn country eight times during this war but has never experienced the terror of being targeted by a Russian drone. A few weeks ago, my friends were on that train. Family Research Council’s Tony Perkins and Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) attended a prayer breakfast alongside me, celebrating Ukraine’s Independence Day. Earlier this month, Dmitry Medvedev, Russia’s Deputy Chairman of the Security Council, warned Western leaders that they would be the Kremlin’s new targets, particularly those traveling to Kyiv by train, the main route to the capital with the airport closed. Ukrainian Railways reported about 40 trains were hit by Russian drones in August alone. His intent is clear. Putin is trying to bully Ukraine’s allies. France’s Emmanuel Macron is taking the threat seriously, warning his security services that Russia’s aggression and threats in Europe are intensifying, citing the train strike and repeated drone incursions into European airspace. Putin threatened Britain for assisting Ukraine with their drone technology. “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which ⁠it will have to answer,” stated the Russian Embassy. Prime Minister Andy Burnham responded by pledging 100% support for Ukraine. “We know he (Putin) is plotting something,” said Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland. “Poland and the Polish people cannot, under any circumstances, afford to be naïve or engaged in wishful thinking. We must base our actions on facts, and those facts are unequivocal.” On Aug. 4, a Russian hybrid drone targeted Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany. The Department of Justice just unearthed a Russian assassination plot in the United States, arresting five men who were ordered to take out a prominent Russian dissident. After learning Putin was considering attacking a NATO ally, the Trump administration dispatched CIA Director John Radcliffe to Moscow to explain there would be consequences to that action. For his part, Trump wanted to believe that Putin was ready to negotiate. The art of the dealmaker has to realize that Putin has never been interested in a deal. The former KGB intelligence officer only understands power and dominance and bullying his way to victory. Trump now has the power to put maximum pressure on Putin. Two weeks ago, he signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Russian Sanctions Act, which allows the U.S. to expand sanctions on Russian military figures and foreign suppliers, to ban U.S. investment in Russia, and tighten restrictions on oil exports to Russia. Trump will have increased authority to impose tariffs on Russian goods. The U.S. will also have more sanctioning authority on those responsible for the abduction of Ukrainian children, which has been a humanitarian cause for first lady Melania Trump. Weakened military might and even weakened resolve by the West led Putin to believe he could roll over his enemies. Putin’s bullying tactics are having the opposite of his intended effects. “We are a nation that may lose territory, but we will never lose our soul; we may surrender territory, but we will never surrender our Homeland,” Nawrocki said. Putin needs to recalculate based on the entrenched support for Ukraine’s allies and Trump’s new authority. He needs to put an end to his war. Bob McEwen is a former member of the U.S. House of Representatives who served on the Intelligence Committee and the U.S. delegation to the European Parliament. He currently serves as the executive director of the Council for National Policy. This article first appeared in the Washington Examiner and is posted here with the kind permission of the author. The UN has said attacks on power stations threaten the health of millions of people in Sudan, who are already facing extreme hunger. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Sudan Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army Agence France-Presse in Khartoum Mon 26 Oct 2026 05.59 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 06.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said. The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity. All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023. The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis. Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning. “My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said. Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams. Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time. In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally. Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people. The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services. Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again. “We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land. Sudan’s RSF committed crimes against humanity in El Fasher, Amnesty says Read more Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year. To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said. Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.
